title: Dynamical Low-Rank Compression of Neural Networks with Robustness under Ad

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The stated bound is not the bound proved. Proposition 2 states κ(S) ≤ exp(R(S)/(2σ_r(S))) + c, with an unspecified additive constant c. But the derivation concludes ln κ(S) ≤ R(S)/(√2 σ_r(S)^2), hence κ(S) ≤ exp(R(S)/(√2 σ_r(S)^2)). The denominator has different units/power of σ_r, the factor differs, and the proof produces no additive constant c. Thus the claimed theoretical guarantee is mathematically inconsistent with its own proof.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proposition 3 and use of ∇R throughout Section 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: R(S)=||S^T S−α_S^2I|| is nondifferentiable when R(S)=0, while Proposition 1 defines ∇R(S)=2S(S^TS−α_S^2I)/R(S), which is 0/0 at exactly those well-conditioned points. Proposition 3 nevertheless defines a gradient-flow ODE involving ∇R(S) without excluding R(S)=0 or defining a subgradient/differential inclusion. The proposition is therefore not well-defined over the stated domain 'for any S'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Definition of regularized loss before Algorithm 1, Eq. (8), and Algorithm 1 lines 5 and 9
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines L̃=L+βR, but the coefficient update uses both −λ∇L̃ and an additional −β∇R. This applies the regularizer twice: once through ∇L̃ and once explicitly. Moreover, the second regularizer term is not multiplied by the learning rate λ. Consequently the displayed update is not gradient descent/Adam on the claimed objective L̃, and the stated theory for L+βR does not describe the implemented algorithm.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.1.1, Eqs. (12)–(13), and all results labeled 'ℓ2-FGSM'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The purported ℓ2-FGSM attack normalizes the input gradient by its infinity norm in Eq. (12), then clamps every coordinate independently to [−ε,ε] in Eq. (13). This is an ℓ∞-style normalization/projection, not an ℓ2-bounded perturbation. A valid ℓ2 FGSM attack must normalize/project using the ℓ2 norm. Therefore the numerous tables and robustness claims labeled ℓ2-FGSM do not evaluate the claimed threat model.

The displayed attack is not an ℓ1-constrained FGSM attack: it takes the elementwise sign of the gradient and divides by a data standard deviation, with no ℓ1 normalization or projection. It is also attributed to [44], Tramèr et al.'s ensemble adversarial training work, which is not a source for the stated 'ℓ1-FGSM' formulation. The paper therefore mislabels and misattributes the attack used for the literature comparison in Table 4.

The numerical columns are mislabeled/shifted. For example, the UCM VGG16 baseline sequence in Table 2 is 86.71, 76.40, 54.96, 89.58, 85.05, 77.77, 37.25, 23.05. Figures 4–6 show that these correspond respectively to FGSM ε=.05, .1, .3; Jitter ε=.035, .045; and Mixup ε=.025, .1, .75. Table 2 instead labels the third number 'Jitter, ε=.3', the fourth 'Jitter, ε=.035', and the fifth 'Mixup, ε=.045'. Thus Table 2 reports attack results under incorrect attack names and strengths.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 versus Figure 4, UCM/VGG16 clean accuracy
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 2 reports UCM VGG16 clean accuracy of 94.40±0.72 for the baseline and 94.61±0.35 for RobustDLRT. Figure 4, explicitly described as the same UCM/VGG16 baseline and low-rank experiment averaged over 10 runs, reports 92.40 for the full-rank baseline and 92.61 for RobustDLRT β=.075. The unregularized DLRT value happens to agree exactly (93.92), making the two-point discrepancy for the other rows especially unexplained.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2, accompanying text in Section 6, and Table 9
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 2 presents one 'RobustDLRT' row per architecture/dataset as though it were one model, but states that it reports the 'best performing β' from Table 9. Table 9 selects different β values separately for FGSM, Jitter, and Mixup. For example, UCM/VGG16 uses β=.075 for FGSM, .2 for Jitter, and .15 for Mixup. The Table 2 values confirm this mixing: VGG16 Jitter ε=.035 value 88.33 is the β=.2 value in Figure 5, while Mixup values such as 90.33 and 70.12 are β=.15 values in Figure 6. A single clean accuracy and compression rate cannot validly characterize this attack-selected composite row. This is post-hoc attack-specific model selection, not a single evaluated defense.

Definition 1 defines R only for a square S∈R^{r×r}. For convolutional layers, however, the paper applies R(Mat(S)^T), where Mat(S)^T has dimensions (r_I S_W S_H)×r_O and is generally rectangular. No rectangular extension of R, its normalization α, its gradient, or the condition-number proof is supplied. The assertion that this is the same regularizer is therefore unsupported by the stated method and theory.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3 discussion of LoRA, Table 1, and Remark 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper correctly states in Section 3 that LoRA 'do[es] not reduce the cost of the full training and inference' because LoRA retains a frozen full-rank base model plus a low-rank update. Yet Table 1 labels a 'LoRA' model as having 95.70% compression, and Remark 1 treats USV^T as the whole LoRA weight matrix. Standard LoRA is W=W0+USV^T, not W=USV^T, so it cannot simultaneously be the cited LoRA method and a 95%-compressed replacement of the full model. The comparison is therefore mislabeled or methodologically inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction contribution 'Preservation of performance' versus Tables 2 and 3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims it proves and empirically verifies that the regularizer 'neither degrades training performance nor reduces clean validation accuracy.' Its own results contradict this. Examples include UCM VGG11 RobustDLRT clean accuracy 93.57% versus baseline 94.23%; CIFAR-10 VGG16 89.49% versus 89.82%; CIFAR-10 ViT-16b 94.66% versus 95.42%; and ImageNet ViT-32l 72.25% versus 74.37%. The claimed universal preservation of clean accuracy must be withdrawn or qualified.

The text admits that baseline and DLRT were trained on static clean data whereas RobustDLRT was trained using adversarial batches, making the comparison confounded. However, Table 6's caption says 'VGG16 is trained on 50% clean images and 50% images attacked,' which implies the protocol applies to all rows. Because the training procedures differ between the compared methods, the table cannot support attribution of RobustDLRT's performance advantage to the proposed regularizer.

The reported black-box experiment attacks the baseline model and transfers those examples to a different low-rank model. It does not test a query-based or adaptive black-box adversary against RobustDLRT. The paper nevertheless says that the low-rank weights 'provide an effective defense against the attack.' High accuracy under non-adaptive transfer examples can reflect transfer failure/model mismatch and is not evidence of black-box robustness against an attacker targeting the defended model.
